items.prose: Three brokers, four orders each, give $F = 4.1538$. The 5% critical value of $F(2, 9)$ is 4.2565.
items.question: What does a 5% test conclude?

options.text: Not significant: $F$ is just below the cut, $p = 0.053$

options.why: Being above 1 is not enough; with 2 and 9 df the cut is 4.2565.
The tail beyond 4.1538 is 0.053, more than 5%.

items.prose: Two algorithms each worked one order in each of 200 stock-days. The orders in a stock-day correlate at 0.8.
items.question: Why does the paired analysis have more power than a two-sample test?

options.text: The shared stock-day noise cancels in each difference
It is robust to fat tails
options.why: The paired $t$ assumes normal differences; robustness to tails is the sign test's strength.
Both estimates are unbiased; the paired one has a smaller standard error.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the two orders of a stock-day share.

explain.text: $\operatorname{Var}(D) = 2\sigma^2(1 - \rho)$, a fifth of the two-sample variance when $\rho = 0.8$.

items.prose: A desk wants to detect $\delta = 2$ bps when shortfall has $\sigma = 10$ bps. The test is two-sided at 5% with 80% power, two independent arms.
items.question: How many orders per arm, rounded up?

items.prose: A team checks a fixed-sample test every evening and stops when $p < 0.05$.
items.question: Why does this raise the false-positive rate?

options.text: Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line, and the test stops at the first crossing
Looking more often lowers the power
options.why: Peeking raises false alarms; it does not lower power.

options.text: The data become biased by being looked at
options.why: Looking does not change the data. Stopping at a lucky moment changes what is reported.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of each look as a new test.

explain.text: With 10 looks the rate is about 19.4%. A sequential test sets its barriers so looking every day keeps the 5%.

items.prose: A pooled two-sample test of two algorithms gives $t = -3.0$.
items.question: What $F$ does a one-way ANOVA of the same two groups give?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With two groups $F = t^2$.

items.prose: Shortfall per order has SD 6 bps, and two orders in a stock-day correlate at $\rho = 0.5$.
items.question: What is the SD of a within-day difference?

explain.text: $\operatorname{Var}(D) = 2 \times 36 \times 0.5 = 36$, so the SD is 6, against 8.49 for unrelated orders.

items.prose: After the experiment, a quant models whether each child order filled (yes or no) on the algorithm used.
items.question: Which model from level 1 fits?

options.text: A binomial GLM with a logit link
A Poisson GLM with a log link
options.why: Poisson is for counts. A yes or no fill is Bernoulli.
Its fitted probabilities can leave $[0, 1]$, as level 1 showed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The outcome is yes or no.

explain.text: A fill is 0 or 1, so the binomial family with the logit link keeps the fill probability in $(0, 1)$.

items.prose: After a significant $F$-test on four brokers, a desk compares every pair.
items.question: What per-test threshold keeps the family-wise error at 5% by Bonferroni?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Four brokers make $\binom42 = 6$ pairs.

byKey.four: You divided by 4, the brokers. There are 6 pairs.

explain.text: Four brokers give $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ pairs, so each is tested at $0.05/6 = 0.00833$.
